                           PRUEBA DE ACCESO A LA UNIVERSIDAD
                                             Curso 2025-2026

                           INSTRUCCIONES GENERALES Y CALIFICACIÓN

Después de leer atentamente el texto y las cuestiones, responda EN INGLÉS a las cinco preguntas.

Las preguntas 1, 4 y 5 ofrecen optatividad: la pregunta 1 presenta 3 cuestiones para elegir 2, la pregunta
4 presenta 6 oraciones para elegir 4 y la pregunta 5 ofrece 2 opciones para elegir solo 1. En aquellos
casos en los que se conteste a más opciones de las pedidas, se corregirán solo aquellas que estén en
primer lugar, descartando el resto.

TIEMPO Y CALIFICACIÓN: 90 minutos. Las preguntas 1, 2 y 4 se calificarán sobre 2 puntos cada una,
la pregunta 3 sobre 1 punto y la pregunta 5 sobre 3 puntos.


                                                 A Style Icon

   Diane Keaton, the Oscar-winning actress whose death at 79 surprised everyone in 2025, was one
   of the last movie stars to arrive in Hollywood before big brands changed the way celebrities
   dressed. She never used a stylist but came with an aesthetic so clearly formed that she shaped
   fashion, rather than allowing fashion to shape her.

   As a result, she was fond of men’s suits, of coats and raincoats as evening wear, and of
   accessories—bowler hats, gloves, belts, glasses. All that is as much a part of her legacy as her
   unforgettable roles in films like Annie Hall (1977)—the film that first introduced the Keaton aesthetic
   to the world—and Reds (1981). In a time when it often seems that movie stars let designers and
   professional brands choose their clothes, Keaton is a reminder that personal style can be powerful.

   Keaton inspired not just her early director, Woody Allen, who famously asked her to dress herself
   for Annie Hall, but also designers such as Ralph Lauren. Her fashion was the impetus for two titles
   from Keaton herself: the 2014 essay collection, Let’s Just Say it Wasn’t Pretty, about finding and
   staying true to your own style, and the 2024 coffee table book, Diane Keaton: Fashion First. Ralph
   Lauren wrote the introduction for the latter. Lauren said he is always being credited with dressing
   Diane in her role as Annie Hall, which could not be further from the truth. He praised her look:
   “Annie’s style was Diane’s style. It’s not defined by the moment. It’s not about trends, but authentic
   and forever.”

   Her affinity for ties, loose trousers, vests and outfits typically worn by men put Keaton in the tradition
   of some old Hollywood female stars who refused to conform to gender or social expectations.
   Those clothes also covered up what she viewed as her weak points. She wore hats, she said,
   because she did not like her hair. Turtlenecks because they hid the neck and framed her face. All
   those layers gave her freedom because they gave her security. “You could call my wardrobe an
   impenetrable castle,” she wrote. Her way of dressing for red-carpet ceremonies was indeed the
   negation to today’s naked dressing trend.

   She never avoided fashion discussions nor rejected the role it played in her life. For her it was not
   frivolous, it was an established part of her identity. Her goal, Keaton wrote, was “finding whatever
   works for you to get out the door every day.” She found it and she encouraged other people to find
   it too. Her style was not for sale, and that made it priceless.

   Adapted from Vanessa Friedman’s “Diane Keaton Was the Definition of a Style Icon: An Appraisal.” The New
   York Times, 12 Oct. 2025. <https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/12/style/diane-keaton-style-icon.html>

                                      Musicians Feel Pain Differently

   It is well known that learning to play an instrument gives advantages beyond music. Research
   shows it is a great activity for the brain. It can improve coordination, speech and memory. It can
   even help to keep our brains younger. Making music is more than a creative skill, it is also a mental
   exercise that strengthens how we think and feel.

   After working with musicians for years, we saw how they kept practising despite feeling pain from
   repeated movements. That made us wonder: if musical training can reshape the brain, can it also
   change how musicians feel pain? Pain activates many reactions in our body and brain. For
   example, touching something hot makes you move your hand immediately. Pain also changes
   brain activity. Usually, it reduces activity in the area of the brain that controls movement. This helps
   you stop using an injured body part too much and protects you in the short term. However, if pain
   continues, problems can appear. For example, if you injure your ankle and avoid using it for weeks,
   mobility decreases and brain activity is disrupted. This can increase pain.

   Research also shows that long-lasting pain can make the brain’s “body map” smaller. This map
   helps the muscles know when and how to move. When the map gets smaller, the pain can feel
   stronger. However, not everyone reacts the same way. Some people tolerate pain better than
   others. In our study, we wanted to find out if musical training changes how musicians deal with
   pain. We created temporary hand pain in musicians and non-musicians. To do this, we used a
   special substance called “nerve growth factor”. This substance is safe but it makes muscles ache
   for days.

   We then measured brain activity by sending small magnetic signals into the brain to see how it
   controls the hand. We made hand maps before the injection, two days later, and eight days later.
   The results were clear. Even before feeling pain, musicians had more detailed hand maps. The
   more hours they practised, the better these maps were. After feeling pain, musicians reported less
   discomfort. In non-musicians, the brain map became smaller after only two days. In musicians, the
   maps stayed the same. The more they had trained, the less pain they felt.

   This was a small study with only 40 people, but findings show that musicians’ brains respond
   differently to pain. Their training seems to protect them.

   Adapted from Ana Zamorano’s “Neuroscience Finds Musicians Feel Pain Differently from the Rest of Us.”
   The Conversation, 24 Sep. 2025. <https://theconversation.com/neuroscience-finds-musicians-feel-pain-
   diﬀerently-from-the-rest-of-us-265815>

b) What are the advantages and disadvantages of practising the same activity for many years, such
   as playing an instrument or doing a sport? Justify your answer.
(Puntuación máxima: 3 puntos)
